title: A full chant
hookLine: the day a kid plays the whole song, not just the chorus: homage, refuges and precepts, start to finish
tomorrow: a month of Pali. what did it actually give you?

lines: WHAT IF I LOSE MY PLACE?
cards: There's a day when a kid who has only ever played the chorus on guitar plays the whole song, first verse to last chord, without stopping. Nothing new gets learned that day. The stringing together is what's new.
Weeks of Pali come to that today: the homage, the refuges and the five trainings, start to finish. And with it comes the fear that rides along with leading anything out loud: what if I lose my place?

teach.h: THE BOW: NAMO TASSA, THREE TIMES.
teach.b: Strung together, the chant has three movements. First, the bow: namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. Homage to him, the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awake.
Second, where you stand: Buddham saranam gacchami, dhammam saranam gacchami, sangham saranam gacchami. To the Buddha, the teaching and the community, I go for refuge.
Then the set again, dutiyampi, a second time, and tatiyampi, a third.
Third, how you'll walk: five trainings, each with the same ending, veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami, I undertake the training to refrain. From taking life. From taking what isn't given.
From sexual misconduct. From false speech. From drink and drugs that cloud the mind into carelessness.
Notice the order. It doesn't open with rules. It opens by honoring someone, then by saying where you shelter, and only then by saying how you'll live.
In a temple, a monk may lead it line by line while the room answers, which is how kids learn it, half a beat behind.
And if you lose your place, the shape finds it for you: bow, refuge, training. Namo, saranam, sikkhapada, pieces from this block, clicking together.

how: At Theravada temples, lay people may begin a visit or a ceremony by chanting the homage, taking the three refuges and the five precepts, repeating each line after a monk who leads.

o: a long chant monks sing alone at the close of the day
homage, refuges and the five trainings, chanted start to finish
every discourse in the Pali canon, sung on one night

games.q: the chant's three movements — tap the pairs.
p: I undertake the training to refrain

s: the chant opens with the five rules
it opens with homage, then refuge, and only then the five trainings.
each of the five trainings ends with the same words
veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami: I undertake the training to refrain.
if you lose your place, the only fix is to start again from namo
the shape finds it: bow, refuge, training. step back in where you are.

games.q: a seven-year-old in the temple class asks why she has to promise not to drink beer. what's a fair answer from the chant itself?
o: she has to, or she isn't a real Buddhist.
it's a training she takes up, samadiyami, about keeping a clear mind.
the fifth line is only for grownups, so she can skip it.
games.why: samadiyami: I undertake. the precepts are trainings taken on, not laws handed down, and the fifth is about what clouds the mind into carelessness.

practice: Chant the whole set from the screen at an easy pace: the homage three times, the refuges three times, then the five trainings. If you lose your place, don't start over; find the shape and step back in.
Then sit in the quiet it leaves.

wordCard.voice: A full chant: homage, refuges and the five trainings, start to finish. A bow, a shelter, a way to walk.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: to the Buddha I go for refuge, the first line of the refuges.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole chant. Bow, refuge, training, and the shape will hold your place. See you tomorrow.
